Chemical Engineering and Processing - Process Intensification

Volume 148, February 2020, 107831

Simultaneous recovery of rare earth elements from waste permanent magnets (WPMs) leach liquor by solvent extraction and hollow fiber supported liquid membrane

Author links open overlay panel
https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cep.2020.107831Get rights and content

Highlights

•

Solvent extraction and HFSLM was applied to REEs recovery from WPMS leach liquor.

•

The optimum parameters were achieved 1 M D2EHPA in isopar L at pH 2.

•

2 mol/L nitric acid as optimum parameters of stripping agent.

•

In the HFSLM system, the optimum transport rate was obtained at 90 min.

•

Separation REEs and iron were successfully demonstrated using HFSLM system.

Abstract

Recovery of rare earth elements (REEs) i.e. neodymium (Nd), dysprosium (Dy), and praseodymium (Pr) from waste permanent magnet (WPMs) leach liquor has been investigated using solvent extraction followed by hollow fiber supported liquid membrane (HFSLM). In the solvent extraction studies, optimum parameters have been obtained for 1 mol/L D2EHPA at pH 2 and 2 mol/L nitric acid for stripping agent. In the HFSLM system, the best percentage achieved at 90 minutes for neodymium, dysprosium, and praseodymium was 58.62 %, 98.46, and 85.59 %, as well as for the recovery 63.13 %, 15.21 %, and 56.29 %, respectively. In this study, the optimum transport rate was achieved at 90 minutes, the transport of rare earth’s ion follows the order was Nd > Pr > Dy. The highest transport and permeability coefficient of rare earths ion was achieved by neodymium with values of 0.0083 min−1 (R2>0.94) and 9.34 × 10-8cm s-1, respectively. According to the results, HFSLM system is a promising and feasible technique for the recovery of REEs and separation REEs from iron in WPMs leach liquor. HFSLM system was successfully applied in the lab-scale for the recycling of REEs from industrial waste materials.

1. Introduction

The rare-earth elements (REEs) have been increasingly crucial in the transition to a recycling economy, because of their major role in various advanced technologies [1,2]. The strongest permanent magnet (NdFeB magnets) containing REEs that are of wide range applications in the various technologies such as electric vehicles, wind power, electronics, computer hard disk, and automobile [[3], [4], [5]]. Over the past two decades, consumption of REEs in high-tech devices has risen to 59 % due to its utilization in various sectors. The global demand for REEs in magnet will increase by 13.2 % according to forecast to reach $41.41 billion by 2022 [6,7]. Even though, consumption and demand are high, only small amounts of REEs are being recycled. The high demand of REEs are causing the critical status of REEs. In recent years, recovery of REEs from industrial waste has been a huge concern in assisting the burden on manufacturers, promoting the recycling economy, preventing environmental pollution by reducing waste amount into the landfill.

The permanent magnet is ascertained as having a significant amount of REEs such as neodymium, dysprosium and praseodymium [[8], [9], [10]]. Therefore, the permanent magnet waste becomes a crucial source of neodymium, dysprosium, and praseodymium and these metals can be recycled. Moreover, commercial recycling of REEs is still extremely low in reality. Therefore, REEs recycling is necessary for in view of the so-called “balance problem” [1]. The researchers have studied the recycling process of REEs from Nd-Fe-B magnets [1]. The various processes of recycling have been expressed in recent years. Various separation techniques are frequently used for REEs recoveries i.e. hydrometallurgy, pyrometallurgy, solvent extraction, chemical precipitation, and ion exchange. The hydrometallurgical process is one of potential mechanism to recycle REEs. However, the main issues are low selectivity because of co-extraction of other non-target elements, high chemical utilize, and generation high quantities of chemical waste [11].

Currently, solvent extraction has been proved to be an efficient technique for the recovery and enrichment of metal ions [12] mainly from leach solutions achieved from the acid leaching [[13], [14], [15]]. Solvent extraction has utilized metallurgy for metal recovery from primary and secondary resources [15]. This technique is the continuous operation that attracts huge concern due to could be eliminate the disadvantages of another technique. Notable advantages of this technique are easy operation, affordable, environmental friendly, quickly, effective separation, works on more concentrated solution, and also feasible to handle larger volumes of dilute pregnant liquors [3,12,15,16].The formation of complexes between ligand molecules soluble in an organic phase and ions is conceptual in this technique [17].

Organophosphorus acid extractants are widely utilized in rare earths extraction [18]. The previous studies was reported that REEs recovery using conventional solvent extraction from NdFeB magnet using various extractants [3,5,15,[19], [20], [21], [22]]. Organophosphorus acids as the main solvent have been widely used for extraction and separation for REEs of NdFeB magnets [20,22].The highest separation factor between the heavy and the light REEs from Nd magnet leachate was used by di(2-ethylhexyl) phosphoric acid (D2EHPA) 0.3 mol/L in hexane [22]. The best separation factor between Dy and Nd with PC88A in 1:1 phase ratio (O/A) was calculated at 125.4 [19]. The optimum concentration for separation Y(III) from Dy(III) was achieved by extractant concentration of PC88A (0.15 mol/L) [2]. The separation of La and Nd from leach liquor containing rare earth metals (REMs) was achieved at 99.99 % using bis(2,4,4-trimethylpentyl) phosphinic acid (Cyanex 272) [23]. Neodymium extraction achieved was 99.79 % with 0.2 mol/L NaCyanex 302 [3]. Two commercial extractants P81R:Cy572 (1:1) 0.3 mol/L in kerosene achieved was 99.99 % Nd(III) recovery with a purity of 99.7 % from an aqueous mixture of Nd/Tb/Dy in chloride medium [20]. The group of extractants most commonly used by industries are D2EHPA, PC88A and Cyanex 272 [17]. The capability of organophosphorus extractants for REEs extraction in decreasing order was D2EHPA < PC88A < Cyanex 272. Nevertheless, the separation factors between adjacent REEs have been depicted to vary corresponding to the decreasing order Cyanex 272 < PC88A < DEHPA [17]. The disadvantage of regular solvent extraction processes such as lean source, environmental effects connected with the loss of organic extractants, loss of diluents in aqueous streams and the formation of third phase could be eliminated by the membrane-based method [24,25].

Supported liquid membrane (SLM) was recognized as the most efficient membranes and advanced technology for the recovery of an element certain due to high selectivity, substantially less inventory of the organic phase, combine of extraction and stripping in one stage [24,26,27]. It also operates on characteristics of non-equilibrium mass transfer where the separation is not limited by the conditions of equilibrium [26]. As a more highly touted technique for membranes, SLMs were investigated in more practical REEs separation applications [28]. In general, the eminent system for the extraction of metal ions was investigated by hollow fiber supported liquid membrane (HFSLM) [29]. HFSLM has many benefits over conventional methods such as adsorption, ion exchange, chemical precipitation, and reverse osmosis, because of lower energy consumption, lower capital, and operating costs, and lower use of solvents [30]. It also provided a higher rate of mass transfer per area of the unit [29,31]. The selective recovery of Nd3+ and Dy3+ from magnetic scrap leach liquor has been performed by ionic liquid-based SLM, a promising application [32]. The high surface area per unit of module volume and high-integrated efficiency was caused HFSLM to achieve significant performance [25]. The previous study revealed that separation of Pr3+ and Nd3+ from mixed rare earth ions using a single stage HFSLM system with various extractants such as Cyanex 272, D2EHPA, PC88A, TOPO and so forth [[33], [34], [35], [36]]. Cyanex 272 and D2EHPA was successfully applied to europium (lanthanides) extraction through SLM [37]. The acidic series extractants were offered high extraction power such as D2EHPA and Cyanex 272 [15,37]. Related to the waste treatment [38], reported that HFSLM was successfully separation of actinides from high-level waste.

Currently, SLM advantages could lead to an intensification of the hydrometallurgical process was employed and very useful for expensive carriers like D2EHPA [37]. The opportunity of using membrane extraction systems for the metal recycling has been recently standing out [39] especially for rare earth elements. Previous studies were successfully extraction of rare earths by HFSLM method are summarized in Table 1. In this study, amongst the effective parameters of the solvent extraction process viz. extractant concentration and feed pH on the simultaneous extraction behavior of neodymium, dysprosium, and praseodymium from waste permanent magnets (WPMs) leach liquor were investigated in this study; as well as the influence of stripping agents and their concentrations were observed. In order to explore the solvent extraction study, kerosene and isopar-L was used as diluent. Furthermore, the optimum parameter from the solvent extraction study has applied in the recovery of neodymium, dysprosium, and praseodymium, as well as separation from an iron element through hollow fiber supported liquid membrane (HFSLM).

2. Material and methods

2.1. Chemical and reagents

The WPMs leach liquor from previous study [8] were conducted to perform solvent extraction study. Di-(2-ethylhexyl) phosphoric acid (D2EHPA) and bis(2,4,4-trimethylpentyl)phosphinic acid (Cyanex 272) as organophosphorus extractants were purchased from Acros Organics and Carbosynth Ltd., respectively. These reagents were used without further purification. Detailed characteristics of the extractants are summarized in Table 2. The extractant diluents such as isopar-L (isoparaffin) and kerosene were supplied by ExxonMobil Chemical and Hayashi Chemical Industries, Ltd., respectively. Sulfuric acid (95–97 %) was purchased from Scharlau, Sodium hydroxide was purchased from PanReac AppliChem. These chemicals were added to adjust the pH solution. Ultra-pure water system of PURELAB flex 3 was used the source for deionized water.

The experimental detail processes for dissolution of the WPMs sample under the optimized conditions were described in the previous study [8]. The composition of the leach liquor is listed in Table 4. In the sample, REEs consist of heavy rare earth elements (HREEs) viz. dysprosium and light rare earth elements (LREEs) viz. neodymium and praseodymium. The main impurity element in the leach liquor was iron, thus its extractions behavior was also investigated in this study.

2.2. Solvent extraction procedures

Solvent extraction was investigated using organophosphorus extractant viz. D2EHPA and Cyanex 272. Kerosene and isopar-L were used as diluents to required extractant concentrations. The required pH of the aqueous solution was adjusted using sodium hydroxide or sulfuric acid solution. Subsequently, the solution was measured by pH meter (SUNTEX SP-2300, 2018). The extraction of REEs was performed by mixing equal volumes of the aqueous phase and organic phase using an orbital shaking incubator (FIRSTEK S300R) at 300 rpm and temperature (25 ± 1 °C) for 20 min. The two phases solution were separated by means of a separation funnel. The temperature could set up and controlled by an orbital shaking incubator (FIRSTEK S300R).

Stripping of element ions from the loaded organic phase was carried out using various mineral acid viz. hydrochloric acid, sulfuric acid, and nitric acid (1−4 mol/L). Stripping was carried out in shake flask with an equal volume of organic and aqueous phase using an orbital shaking incubator at 300 rpm and temperature (25 ± 1 °C) for 10 min.

In the solvent extraction study, extraction efficiency (%E), distribution ratio (D), separation factor (β), Stripping ratio (St) are calculated in Eqs. (1), (2), (3), (4) as follows :(1)E%=[C]0-[C]t[C]0x100(2)D=[C]org[C]aq(3)β=DADB(4)St%=[C]aq[C]orgWhere [C]0 and [C]t represents to the initial and at time t aqueous phase concentrations, respectively, of REEs ions. [C]org is the concentration of REEs in loaded organic phase. DA and DB respectively denote the distribution ratio of metal A and B. The loaded organic phase was stripped by stripping agent of equal volume. The REEs concentration in the aqueous phase was quantified to assess stripping rate (St), [C]org stands for the concentration of REEs in the loaded organic phase.

2.3. Supported liquid membranes procedures

The hollow fiber module was a Liqui-Cel® membrane contractor, Extra-Flow 2.5 × 8 (X-50 microporous hollow fiber membrane contactor purchased from Membrana (Charlotte, U.S.A.). The hollow fiber supported liquid system (HFSLM) consisted of two variable flow rate controllers, two gear pumps, four pressure gauges, two rotameters. The schematic diagram of single module HFSLM apparatus is shown in Fig. 1 and the HFSLM characteristics [40] is depicted in Table 3.

The transport experiments were carried out using hollow fiber supported liquid membrane (HFSLM). The HFSLM system consists of two mixing tanks; one for aqueous feed phase (waste permanent magnet leach liquor) and another tank for the strip phase contains organic solution (1 mol/L D2EHPA in isopar L) and a stripping agent (2 mol/L HNO3). In order to maintain a solution is homogeneous, organic solution and stripping agent in the strip phase tank was stirred at 300 rpm at room temperature, as well as the aqueous feed phase tank. The WPMs leach liquor as an aqueous feed phase containing REEs to be extracted was kept at pH 2. The organic phase easily dispersed on the shell side surface of the hollow polypropylene microporous fibers then the aqueous feed phase flowed in the tube side surface. The feed flow rate and organic solution flow rate was set up at 200−250 ml/min and 250−300 ml/min, respectively. The ratio of feed solution, organic solution and strip solution in HFSLM system is 4:2:1. Samples were taken from the feed phase and strip phase every 15 min. The concentration of REEs in the aqueous phase was determined by an inductively coupled plasma-atomic emission spectrometry (ICP-AES, Shimadzu ICPE-9800 series).

3. Theoretical background

3.1. Transport of rare earth (RE) ions across the liquid membrane phase

RE ions extraction through HFSLM was facilitated by coupling counter-transport using an extractant. The organic extractant dissolved in the organic solvent is stuck in the hydrophobic micropores of hollow fibers as the liquid membrane. The rare earth ions in the aqueous feed and the aqueous stripping are commonly fed counter-currently in HFSLM tube and shell sides, respectively. As shown in Fig. 2 depicts that RE ions transport to across in the liquid membrane phase. In Eq. (5) describes that at the feed liquid membrane interface occurs extraction process when the organic extractant ((HA)2) reacts with the RE ions in the feed phase to form the complex species and hydrogen ions [22,41]:(5)RE(aq)3++3HA¯2(org)⇌REA3HA3¯+3H+

Afterwards, due to the concentration gradient between the two interfaces, the complex species diffuses across the liquid membrane phase to the liquid membrane-stripping interface. Later on, the stripping reaction takes place as in Eq. (6). Thus, the rare earth ions are released into the stripping phase. Subsequently, the rare earth ions and hydrogen ions are counter-transported across the liquid membrane phase [29,42].(6)REA3HA3¯+3H+⇌REaq3++3HA¯2(org)where (aq) states the species in the aqueous phase and (org) states the species in the liquid membrane phase, (HA)2 is the dimer from of D2EHPA. The overbar depicts the species in the liquid membrane phase. Transportation of rare earth ions across the HFSLM system is illustrated in Fig. 2.

The rate of mass transfer via the liquid membrane can be described by the permeability times the driving force for extraction, which relies on both sides of the membrane concentration. If the driving force is high, only the concentration in the feed phase suffices to describes the process [43,44]. Assuming partition coefficients of the metal species at the membrane aqueous feed solution interface that are much larger than those at the membrane-aqueous strip solution interface, the flux (J) could be calculated by using the following equation [45](7)J=PfCfwhere Pf is the permeability coefficient at the feed membrane interface and Cf is the rare earth ion concentration at the feed side. The flux can alternatively be expressed as(8)J=-1Q.dVfCfdtwhere Vf is the feed volume and Q is the effective area of the membrane. Under assumption of negligible change in the feed volume, Eqs. (7) and (8) could be integrated to achieve(9)lnCf,tCf,0=-AVfPt

Cf,0 and Cf,t describe the feed concentration at initial and at time t, respectively. A is represented as the membrane area. The permeability (P) values were calculated using Eq. (9). This equation shows that the concentration decreases exponentially time since the permeability coefficient is concentration-independent.

In this study, the recovery percentage of REEs was calculated based on the following equation:(10)R%=[Cst]t[Vst][Cf]0[Vf]x100%Where [Cst]t and [Vst] represent the concentration of aqueous strip at time t and volume of aqueous strip, respectively. [Cf]0 and [Vf] represent an initial concentration of aqueous feed and volume of aqueous feed, respectively.

4. Result and discussion

4.1. Influences of aqueous pH in solvent extraction

The influences of pH on REEs extraction are shown in Fig. 3. The influences of pH on the extraction of REEs by D2EHPA and Cyanex 272 with different diluents was investigated at different initial pH of aqueous solutions ranging from 1 to 2.5. The concentration of extractant and O/A phase ratio were kept constant at 0.25 mol/L and 1:1, respectively. The pH of aqueous medium enormously influences the elements’ extraction in this study due to that D2EHPA and Cyanex 272 as organophosphorus acid are cation exchangers which produce H+ ions causing the decrease in pH which afterward declines the extraction of elements.

In the pH range of 1–1.5, the REEs extraction slightly decreases for the extractants in isopar-L. The extraction behavior of LREEs with organophosphorus acid extractants was almost similar to each other but different to the extraction behavior of HREEs. The extraction of HREEs was higher than LREEs. The optimum pH for REEs extraction was occured at pH 2 is D2EHPA in isopar-L as optimum extractant due to its lower extraction of iron as the impurity (less than 60 %). Whereas, Cyanex 272 in its diluents was accomplished more than 60 % of iron extraction (this extraction exceeded REEs extraction). The optimum extractions achieved by D2EHPA in isopar-L at pH 2 of Nd, Dy and Pr were 72.5 %, 81.8 %, and 73.7 %, respectively. The reliance of extraction efficiency of rare earths on the value of pH may be associated with the changes of H+ concentration released by acidic extraction [46]. Hence, to prevent the high iron extraction, further experiments were kept at pH 2.

Commonly, rare earths ion extraction from aqueous media by cation exchange extractants such as D2EHPA and Cyanex 272 in Eq. (11) is expressed as [47](11)RE3++3H¯A⇌RE¯A3+3H+

RE denotes any elements and A is the organic anion. However, the extraction process is more arduous as the acidic extractants as dimers in non-polar organic solutions and the rare earth complexes formed during extraction may contain undissociated organic molecule as given in Eq. (12) [48].(12)RE3++3H2A2¯⇌REHA23¯+3H+Here H2A2 refers to the dimeric form of the organic phase. From inspection of Eqs. (11), (12) it is evident that the extraction of rare earths with cation exchangers is promoted by increasing the aqueous phase pH [16].

The extraction of REEs from WPMs leach liquor was conducted by ion exchange mechanism. The graphical method was used for identification of REEs solvent extraction reaction. The slope of plots of the logarithmic distribution ratio of REEs versus pH relates to the number of hydrogen ions involved in the exchange reaction. The plots of Log DREEs versus equilibrium pH are depicted in Fig. 5a. The plots are linear with slope values of 0.26, 0.95, and 0.82 for Dy, Nd, and Pr, respectively. These indicated the release of 1 mol of H+ ion leading to extraction of REEs. The bridging ions enhanced the formation of REEs multinuclear species that was served by chloride ions.

The distribution ratios of REEs increase as the pH of aqueous phase increases. This is associated with the cationic activity of the extractants and exhibits that REEs are extracted by a cation-exchange process whereby hydrogen ions are released by the reaction [2]. The leach liquor of REEs from WPMs contain chloride solutions, thus those REEs ions are extracted as mixed complexes including chloride together with extractants. The chloride complexes of LREEs are more stable than HREEs due to the interaction of borderline to soft chloride ion with polarizable LREEs [2]. Hence, in this mechanism, the slopes are less than 3 and there are differences in the slopes of REEs.

4.2. Influences of extractant concentration in solvent extraction

REEs were extracted by varying the concentrations of organophosphorus acid from 0.25 to 1 mol/L. The extraction experiments were carried out using O/A ratio of 1:1 at temperature of ± 25 °C for 20 min at pH 2. The influences of extractant concentration on the extraction of REEs are depicted in Fig. 4. Commonly, the REEs extraction increases with increasing extractant concentration. These experiments endeavor that the extractions are being selective for REEs and iron as an impurity is deficient being co-extracted. In this case, the REEs extraction was more effective using D2EHPA than Cyanex 272. It was found that iron element could be co-extracted more than 60 % in all extraction conditions used, except D2EHPA in isopar-L. Besides REEs were selectively extracted over iron under D2EHPA in isopar-L. As shown in Fig. 4, the iron extraction using Cyanex 272 achieved was more than 75 % that even exceeds REEs extraction. In this case, the result indicates that D2EHPA in isopar-L used are selective for REEs due to the extraction percentages for REEs being greater than iron. According to the result, 1 mol/L D2EHPA in isopar-L is selective for REEs extraction with extractions of 81.55 %, 83.5 % and 87.93 % for dysprosium, neodymium and praseodymium, respectively. D2EHPA has low solubility and strong activity in organic solvent-water interfaces [49]. In terms of extraction performance, amongst the organophosphorus extractant group, the organophosphorus acids such as D2EHPA are favored due to having extraction energy higher than phosphinic (Cyanex 272) and phosphonic. Furthermore, D2EHPA are strongly acidic extractants so that readily dissociate enabling high loading [50]. D2EHPA have structures alkoxy (–RO) group directly attached to the phosphorus atom. This structure significantly affects the extractability and the separation efficiency of metal ions [51].

D2EHPA might be feasible for the recovery of REEs from WPMs leach liquor by dint of the REEs extraction being higher than element impurity than when using Cyanex 272 at the same time conditions. The result of present study as also in accordance with the previous study which revealed that D2EHPA is the most effective and propitious extractants for recycling of magnet REEs [17]. This study investigated that D2EHPA has higher selectivity to REEs, instead of iron in the aqueous solution. Therefore, D2EHPA was chosen as a feasible extractant for recovery of REEs and 1 mol/L D2EHPA in isopar-L was considered as an optimum concentration for further experiments.

The sequence of extraction of between dysprosium as HREEs and LREEs such as neodymium and praseodymium follows the atomic number, which can be explained by considering the ionic radii and charge density of dysprosium, neodymium, and praseodymium. The ionic radius of dysprosium is smaller than that of neodymium and praseodymium due to the lanthanide contraction [2,13,22,52]. The outcome will correspondingly be the increased charge density with the decreasing ion radius. The smaller ion can contribute to the ion REEs binding to the extractants molecule, controlled by a cation-exchange mechanism, promoting the extraction of the HREEs in preference over the LREEs [22]. The extraction of dysprosium as HREEs is higher compared to neodymium and praseodymium as LREEs due to the charge density of dysprosium being higher than that of neodymium and praseodymium (Fig. 4).

As shown in Fig. 5a, the distribution ratio (D) increase eventually as pH increase in the aqueous phase. It is caused by D2EHPA cationic character and denoted that REEs are extracted with a cation-exchange mechanism in which hydrogen ions are released through the reaction. The slope analysis is a long-established and effective procedure to obtain stoichiometric constants and equilibrium and information about extraction processes. The examination of the variation of the distribution ratio as a function of the relevant experimental variables is the basis of this analysis [53]. The graph plot of log DREEs versus log extractant concentration is shown in Fig. 5b. The extraction stoichiometry of Dy, Nd and Pr was observed by straight lines with the slope values of -0.016, 0.46, 0.67, respectively. It is noticed that 1 extractant molecule is involved in the REEs extraction reactions. The slope of dysprosium is negative because of the formation of dysprosium-chloride complexes occurring concurrently with the decrease in dysprosium concentrations. In this study, extraction of metals from solutions containing chloride ions is complex. REEs would form a chloro-complex as the high concentration of HCl that is likely to react with extractants. The common expression for the formation of chlorocomplexes in the aqueous phase was inferred in Eq. (13) [54](13)M2++nCl-→MCln2-n

Furthermore, the extraction of REEs can be expressed based on the high chloride concentration in the aqueous phase was depicted in Eq. (14) [55](14)M3++3Cl-+12HA2⇌MCl3.HA

In the present study, the slope value is 1, these indicates the scheme of REEs chelate formation is REECl3.H2A2. According to this result, it may be inferred that Eq. (15) represents the solvent extraction reaction of REEs with acidic extractant at higher acidity in this study(15)REECl3+H2A2¯⇌REECl3H2A2¯+H+

4.3. Stripping studies

The loaded organic phase achieved in cases of optimum extraction of REEs was carried out for stripping with various mineral acids viz. sulfuric acid (H2SO4), hydrochloric acid (HCl), and nitric acid (HNO3) and their concentrations (1−4 mol/L) at O/A ratio of 1:1. The percentage of stripping was plotted in Table 5 HNO3 can be supposed as a propitious stripping agent since it points to best stripping of REEs almost completely in a single stage for neodymium and praseodymium (98.97 % and 99.37 %) was achieved by using 2 mol/L. Choosing a proper acid type as a stripping agent was critical. In this study, the stripping efficiency of nitric acid was higher than sulfuric acid and hydrochloric acid due to nitric acid is a powerful oxidizing inorganic acid [46]. Previous studies reported that stripping of lanthanum were successfully achieved by nitric acid as stripping agent [46,56,57].

4.4. REEs recovery using hollow fiber supported liquid membrane

The HFSLM system was conducted after optimization of experimental variables from quantitative recovery of REEs in solvent extraction. 1 mol/L D2EHPA in isopar-L with pH 2 of WPMs leach liquor have been chosen to REEs recovery by HFSLM system. The aqueous feed contains 2707 mg/L neodymium, 155 mg/L dysprosium, 857 mg/L praseodymium, and 5991 mg/L iron as impurity. Fig. 6 shows the transport of rare earth ions using 1 mol/L D2EHPA in isopar-L using HFSLM as a function time. As shown in Fig. 6, the concentration of rare earth ions in the aqueous feed significantly decreased from neodymium from 2707 mg/L to 457 mg/L, dysprosium from 155 mg/L to 35 mg/L, praseodymium 857 mg/L to 215 mg/L within 240 min, respectively. The decreasing of concentration rare earth ions in the aqueous feed phase was observed because of their selective extraction by D2EHPA as extractant. The rare earth ions in the aqueous feed phase interacted to the organic solvent on the membrane surface, they formed a complex organic metal compound and were transferred to the aqueous strip phase by the difference of H+ concentration between the aqueous feed and the aqueous strip. In the present study, HFSLM system was carried out to extract and recover of REEs simultaneously from WPMs leach liquor. The extraction of neodymium, dysprosium, and praseodymium in the aqueous feed within 90 min was achieved 58.62 %, 98.46 %, and 85.59 %, respectively. Whereas the recovery of neodymium, dysprosium, and praseodymium in the aqueous feed within 90 min was achieved 63.13 %, 15.21 % and 56.29 %. Moreover, HFSLM system can increase the neodymium and praseodymium concentration in the aqueous strip approximately 2.3 times higher than the initial concentration in the aqueous feed within 90 min. The concentration of neodymium and praseodymium in the aqueous strip was calculated 6834 mg/L and 1929 mg/L, respectively.

Different behaviors were observed for rare earth ions. As shown in Fig. 6, the result reveals that during the 90 min, more extractant is available at the feed/liquid membrane interface, leading to an efficient transport ion of rare earths. However, when the extractant content is lower because its exchange and dissolution, the dysprosium as HREEs extraction is favored than neodymium and praseodymium as LREEs due to the charge density of dysprosium being higher than that of neodymium and praseodymium. The smaller ion can contribute to the rare earth ions binding to the extractants molecule, controlled by a cation-exchange mechanism, promoting the extraction of the HREEs in preference over the LREEs [22]. The optimum transport rate was achieved at 90 min. After 90 min’ operation, the transport rate was insignificantly increased, even the transport of dysprosium ions stops as soon as the equilibrium was reached. It is indicated that pseudo steady state diffusion has occurred in this study. In this case, HFSLM system more selective to recovery neodymium and praseodymium than from WPMs leach liquor due to the dysprosium recovery percentage was obtained only 15.21 %. According to the following order of rare earth transport, the transport of rare earths ion in this study following the order was Nd > Pr > Dy. Similar result with previous study reported that decreasing of transport ion with increase in lanthanide number is because the formation of stronger complex in the lanthanide series that occurs because decease in ionic radii [58]. However, in this study, the highest transport of rare earth ions was achieved by neodymium because it is probable that D2EHPA more selective with neodymium (Fig. 6).

Hollow fiber supported liquid membrane system was found to be an appropriate process for the simultaneous extraction and recovery of REEs from WPMs leach liquor. As can be seen in Fig. 6, the results revealed that REEs were selectively extracted and recovered from WPMs leach liquor. It is indicated that the HFSLM system is beneficial for the separation of REEs from iron as an impurity metal that is commonly complicated in the regular solvent extraction. Hence, this study obviously proves that HFSLM method is selectively feasible for REEs recovery in the industrial field.

As shown in Fig. 2, the transport of rare earth ions across the liquid membrane phase from the aqueous feed to the aqueous strip involves the three steps: (1) rare earth ions diffuse through the aqueous feed boundary layer and react with the carried at feed-membrane interface resulting in the formation of rare earth complex, (2) the rare earth complex diffuses through the membrane to the stripping phase due to concentration gradient of the rare earth complex, (3) the rare earth is released to the stripping phase at the membrane-strip interface [59]. The proton transport could be a way to promote rare earth ions co-transport while leaving the iron ions in the feed phase and leading to a high selectivity for rare earth ions [60]. reported that the metal-carrier complex is formed at the feed/liquid membrane interface, creating a permanent concentration gradient through the membrane, which allows the enrichment of the transported substance in the receiving phase in facilitated transport. The plot of lnCf,tCf,0 versus time for the diffusion of rare earth ions through the HFSLM system in 90 min is presented in Fig. 7. The chemical transformations rates might control transport kinetics through the liquid membrane, depending on transport mechanism. The rates of chemical reactions of neodymium, dysprosium, and praseodymium was calculated 0.0083 min−1(R2>0.94), 0.0128 min−1(R2 >0.98), and 0.0096 min−1(R2>0.94) respectively. The dysprosium slope is greater than neodymium and praseodymium, it is indicated that dysprosium ion transfer from aqueous feed to the aqueous strip is more quickly than neodymium and praseodymium. By the slope, the permeability coefficient value could be calculated using Eq. lnCf,tCf,0. The permeability coefficient and flux value for each REEs in the experiment were depicted in Table 6. The main concerns HFSLM system is related to membrane stability. The flux is higher than the permeability coefficient as shown in Table 7. This phenomenon occurs likely the membrane is slightly losing hydrophobicity characteristics.

5. Conclusion

Solvent extraction and hollow fiber supported liquid membrane (HFSLM) have been applied and investigated for simultaneous extraction and recovery of rare earth elements (REEs) from waste permanent magnets (WPMs) leach liquor. In the solvent extraction method, D2EHPA in isopar-L was obviously proven to have the best extraction capacity for REEs in WPMs leach liquor under all experimental conditions. 1 mol/L D2EHPA in isopar-L at initial pH of 2 was selected for REEs extraction. Dysprosium, neodymium, and praseodymium extraction was achieved at 81.55 %, 83.5 % and 87.93, respectively with the iron extraction approximately at 56.67 %. It is concluded that D2EHPA diluted with isopar-L is more selective to be used as an extractant for REEs recovery from WPMs leach liquor. The REEs extraction mechanism by slope analysis depicts that one molecule D2EHPA as extractant is involved in the solvent extraction of one molecule for each REEs. The stripping of REEs loaded organic phase was observed by utilizing 2 mol/L nitric acid which was the best concentration for stripping. In the HFSLM system, the extraction of neodymium, dysprosium, and praseodymium in the aqueous feed within 90 min was obtained at 58.62 %, 98.46 %, and 85.59 %, respectively. Whereas, neodymium, dysprosium, and praseodymium recovery were obtained 63.13 %, 15.21 %, and 56.29 %, respectively without co-extraction of iron elements as an impurity. The chemical reactions rate of neodymium, dysprosium, and praseodymium was calculated 0.0083 min−1 (R2>0.94), 0.0128 min−1 (R2 >0.98), and 0.0096 min−1 (R2>0.94) respectively. Whereas, the permeability coefficient of neodymium, dysprosium, and praseodymium was achieved at 9.34 × 10-8, 1.38 × 10-7 and 8.33 × 10-8, respectively. Finally, this study clearly proved that the HFSLM method was successfully applied in the lab-scale for the recycling of REEs from industrial waste materials.
